Pretty Derby, Ugly Grind – A Tedious Experience Disguised as Charm Umamusume: Pretty Derby might lure you in with cute characters and flashy presentation, but once you dive into the gameplay, the illusion quickly fades. Beneath the glossy surface is a grind-heavy, repetitive mess that punishes players more often than it rewards them. 1. Repetitive Loop with Minimal Payoff At its core, the game revolves around raising horse girls (the "Umamusume") by sending them through training sessions, races, and events. Unfortunately, the gameplay loop quickly becomes stale. Each training cycle takes a significant amount of time and involves minimal strategy, often boiling down to "pick the stat that went up the most last time." Worse, most of the outcomes are heavily RNG-dependent—meaning your success often hinges on luck, not skill. 2. Heavy Time Investment, Low Reward Raising a character to a competitive level can take hours of grinding, only to be met with underwhelming results due to bad event RNG or stat imbalances. You’ll often need to repeat the same cycle dozens of times just to get a slightly better outcome. The game expects a ridiculous time commitment for incremental progression, which makes it feel more like a chore than a game. 3. Gacha System is Brutally Unforgiving Like many mobile games, Umamusume is built around a gacha system, but this one is particularly ruthless. Unlocking and properly raising top-tier characters requires significant investment—either in time or real money. Even then, the support card system adds another layer of gacha grinding, where you're not just pulling for characters, but also the tools to make them viable. This two-tier gacha setup turns the game into a pay-to-compete experience, especially in events or PvP races. 4. Stale Content and Poor Progression Pacing While new characters and events are added periodically, they rarely change the underlying mechanics. The core gameplay doesn’t evolve, so even with fresh content, you're still stuck doing the same grind with slightly different animations or dialog. The slow drip of progression makes it hard to stay engaged unless you're deeply invested in the franchise or its characters. 5. Lack of Player Agency Despite the number of options you’re presented with during training runs, the game offers very little real agency. Your choices often feel meaningless when RNG can derail your entire run due to a random failed training, injury, or bad stat roll. Strategy takes a backseat to dice rolls, making success feel arbitrary and frustrating. Verdict: Umamusume: Pretty Derby could have been a fun blend of simulation and strategy with its unique concept, but it’s buried under a mountain of grind, poor pacing, and RNG-heavy systems. What should feel like a race turns into a slow, punishing slog. Unless you're a diehard fan of the franchise or a gacha masochist, this game is likely to wear out its welcome fast. 2/5 – Cute but exhausting.

I tried. God, I tried. I gave her the best shoes, the best meals, trained her under the clearest skies, and yet… she lost. She stumbled on the final corner, and I stumbled as a trainer, no, as a human being. How do I look her in the eyes after this? Those bright, hopeful eyes that once sparkled with dreams of victory… now clouded with tears. “I’ll win next time, Trainer!” she said, forcing a smile through her trembling lips — but I knew it was for my sake. I wasn’t just training a racer. I was nurturing a dream. And I crushed it with my incompetence. I picked the wrong races. I misjudged her stats. I overtrained when she needed rest. I failed to notice she was tired. I failed to see she needed a break. I failed… her. The crowds cheered for another, but I heard nothing. Just the sound of her hooves slowing, her breath short, her heart breaking. And mine with it. If you're reading this… cherish your horsegirl. Don’t make the same mistakes I did. Because sometimes, it's not the race you lose — It’s her trust.

I've played many gacha games for varying lengths of time, and at first I was really in love with this one. The characters are cute and cool, the writing is pretty good overall (especially if you like sports animes), and the core roguelike loop feels more like an actual game than a rote daily task (at least for as much as I've played so far.) However, I just experienced the first event change-over, and it feels *horrible*. For anyone not familiar with gacha game SOP: The bread and butter of most gacha games is limited-time events, each focused on a specific SSR character. Correspondingly that character will be the focus of the event gachapon pull, with a higher chance that any SSR pull will be the event character. Since pulls are still random though, typically there will be a guaranteed way to get the event character, which is [Gain a token for each event pull; trade in X event pull tokens for the event character]. This is all true in U:PD, and here, X is 200. So after 200 pulls in any event, you are guaranteed that event's SSR character. It's an important fail-safe to prevent too much player dissatisfaction from long unlucky streaks. One important thing that differs from gacha game to gacha game is the answer to "What happens to unspent event gacha points when the event ends?" In other words, if you did 150 gacha pulls during an event, what happens to those 150 event points? The only transaction established is 200 EP = free SSR event character. Answers to that question range from "You lose those points and gain nothing" to "Those event points become generic pull points, where you exchange 200 generic points for a random SSR character". Umamusume: Pretty Derby falls on the "you lose the points and gain nothing" side of things. You technically don't gain *nothing*--what you actually get is a generic currency, "clovers", where 200 clovers = 1 generic gacha pull. So, rather than 200 points guaranteeing an SSR character, instead you get 200 points gives you one free random pull. I don't know the exact pull rates in this game, but from my experience so far I'd guess it's a ~2% chance for an SSR. In other words, for the expected value of 1 SSR you'd need 50 pulls, which means 50*200= 10,000 clovers. It's a complete leg-sweep (which is bad for horses!) of the excitement and anticipation about getting a new character. Remember that these event points are meant to work as a failsafe to ensure players don't feel like all their hopes and effort went unrewarded if they get hit by a string of bad luck. Losing that feels very bad. So, all that said, it's important to keep in mind for this game that you should never do an event pull unless you have stored up enough currency to do *200* pulls. It's 1500 carats per 10-pull, so 20*1500= 30,000 carats. Spend any less than that at a time and you might end up losing it all for nothing. It's a shame that such an otherwise good gacha game decided to go with a predatory and punishing event point system.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1] [i]Umamusume: Pretty Derby[/i] stands out with its quality presentation, endearing characters and uplifting story tone - a refreshing change from the often grim narratives in these games. While its incremental progression can be satisfying, the experience quickly wears thin due to excessive and repetitive grind, stingy gacha, and RNG-laden progression system, all worsened by the global version’s accelerated schedule which makes it hard to recommend even from a casual perspective. Note: this review is based on the current version and I do not consider it reasonable to expect players to endure a sub-par experience for months or years until some QoL gets ported from the JP version. Shoutout to Golshi, Nature, Fukukitaru and Urara. [h1]Gameplay[/h1] At its core, the game is a training simulation game with a PvP layer on top. While this genre isn’t widely popular outside of some niche markets, you can find a similar experience with series such as Princess Maker, Tokimeki Memorial, Monster Rancher, Idolmaster, and even draw some comparison with the life sim aspect of the Persona games. The career mode begins by selecting a story scenario, a trainee Umamusume, two legacy horses to pass on their stats and skills, and a deck of "support cards" which represent other characters who can influence training outcomes and provide passive benefits and skills. Each career spans three in-game years divided into 70-ish turns, framed by the scenario and trainee's storyline during which you raise stats, manage rest, and participate in races, while navigating an extensive amount of VN segments that deepen character and story progression. Training depends on a web of factors such as friendship levels with the support card characters, stat affinities, prior training frequency, and card synergies, making the loop engaging and skill-based with an element of risk and reward. The horse races themselves serve as both a test and a spectacle, albeit one with no player intervention. The simulation is surprisingly complex and it blends stats, skills and a big dose of RNG into surprisingly exciting events. They're fully animated, complete with dynamic commentary and if you win, charming animated idol performances that even a cold-hearted person like myself could enjoy from occasionally, especially after a difficult run. A career ends when all the milestones have been met or upon failing one of them. The Uma gets a snapshot with her final stats and skills and a random set of traits she can pass on when used as a legacy horse. She can also be used in PVP matches and a few daily farming races, which seem to be the only content for the foreseeable future. As someone with a low interest in PVP, the payoff for the training is very limited even if the strategic element of career training can be cerebral. That said, the system's flaws become apparent quickly. A run takes 30+ minutes even with autoskip, and daily stamina allows almost five of them. Progress relies heavily on RNG without strong prep and losing races can feel arbitrary, with outcomes varying wildly when using race retries. Stat inheritance and post-career “spark” traits are highly randomized, which leads to high grind for a low payoff. [h1]Story[/h1] This is, in my opinion, the game’s strongest aspect. There's a huge amount of VN-style content for a gacha: each character has a unique career story, and both support cards and scenarios add randomized events that flesh out the cast. Despite its age, the game features expressive 3D animations, the main content is voiced and it has solid production value overall. Bond stories act as a career prologue, giving players a taste of each character’s personality before deciding whether to train or pull for them. That said, the main story, careers, events, and the anime are all separate continuities, which may be disappointing if you want a cohesive overarching plot. The characters themselves lean hard into anime archetypes: and most can be summed up in a few words, with careers that follow a predictable rise-fall-rise structure. That said, the stories are still charming, heartwarming, and surprisingly effective at making you care. You’ll almost certainly find someone you like, just don't expect much depth there. [h1]Presentation[/h1] Visually and technically, the PC port is excellent with one major caveat: the game forcibly installs on your C: drive regardless of your Steam directory, which is infuriating. (Bonus: It ALSO won't remove those files on uninstall). Beyond that, stability and performance is solid (concerts aside), the clean 3D anime aesthetic works well despite asset reuse, and the soundtrack is catchy and varied (BAKUSHIN!). Menus are snappy, the UI is responsive, and the game generally looks and feels polished. Unfortunately, this is dragged down by the abysmal in-game communication. Stats are vaguely explained, skills lack numbers or clear effects, and some are outright misleading in their description. You can upgrade skills, but the game won’t tell you how effective it is and the race mechanics are never fully intuitive which, combined with the heavy dose of RNG, make careers frustrating without external info. While wikis and planners do a great job filling the gap, it’s unacceptable that even the most basic systems require external info to understand making the barrier to effective play unnecessarily high. [h1]Gacha and progression[/h1] The gacha is rough, even by gacha standards. It’s a four year old Japanese gacha design with split banners (characters and support cards), a 0.5/0.75% rate-up, and hard spark at 200 pulls with no pity or carryover. You can expect one spark every 2 to 3 months depending on your dedication and PVP focus and the accelerated Global schedule also means fewer daily gem sources, making those estimates optimistic. Support cards are essential for strong career runs to mitigate RNG, and many only reach full potential after multiple limit breaks, making dupes highly impactful as well. That makes the system heavily P2W in PVP and leaves F2P players skipping most banners. The only upside is the ability to plan ahead using knowledge from the JP server. Outside of gacha, progression involves leveling characters and cards, limit breaking with dupes or (slowly farmable) shards, and building up legacy horses but this ties directly into the game’s heavy grind. Legacy "sparks" (traits passed down) have single digit chances of being useful, meaning you’ll repeat careers dozens of times for tiny improvements. Combined with how much support cards affect stat growth, success often comes down to heavy time investment to offset RNG or owning meta cards. Events have a similar issue: Global’s first two required around three full career runs per day over two weeks to max the free event card, assuming you succeeded each time. Unsurprisingly, bonuses were tied to SSR cards/characters, pushing players toward whaling for a faster grind. [h1]A word on social pressure[/h1] Given the game’s sudden popularity, this deserves a mention. The game's release blew up thanks to high marketing, positive review bombing from longtime fans, and a generous early-game honeymoon period and the result is a wave of new players jumping in out of FOMO, clout-chasing, or just not wanting to miss out, but this is a hard game to recommend casually: the grind is intense, the gacha unforgiving, and the time investment steep. Once the launch bonuses dry up, you’re stuck running the same 30-minute careers endlessly, praying for good sparks and saving gems for months just to pull one unit you like or some copies of a meta card while also dealing with the accelerated schedule so take a moment to consider whether this is the kind of loop you’ll still want to engage with for months in a row. Many gacha players have a huge tolerance towards excusing poor practices but this shouldn't be the expected norm.

Fun gameplay loop, but the game [b]does NOT respect your time OR money.[/b] It's a gacha game, so it's already predatory in nature, but even among gacha systems, this one's exceedingly punishing and outdated. 200 draws for a pity, rate-up is 0.750%, pity counter does NOT carry over across banners, there are NO further rate-up boosts if you fail to pull any of the rate-ups, and if you fail to pull a multiple of 200 times on any banner, your pull currency is converted into clovers - a worthless currency where you can exchange the equivalent of 200 draws for a single draw ticket (yes, 200 : 1 exchange rate). At its core, it's a roguelike stat raising game... but the meta progression is abysmal. The gameplay really boils down to nested layers of RNG: Did your assists show up on the right training stations (rainbow training)? Did you get the skills you wanted from chain events (some of them are RNG to get the gold skill) or skill hints (!)? Did you avoid getting random negative status conditions and mood downs during your run? Did the infirmary actually remove the negative status conditions you were randomly afflicted with? Did your uma get blocked by the NPC horses with half of your stats, causing you to lose the race? At the end of the run, did you avoid the 20% chance to get a Guts blue spark (even if your other stats are all jacked)? Did you RNG the pink spark you wanted, with a high enough star rating (purely random)? Did you get the skill and race sparks you wanted (more RNG)? Not to mention, the Global version has NONE of the quality of life features available on the Japanese version, so it feels like playing a beta version of the game. And despite the ~40% accelerated release schedule, Global has received NO exclusive premium currency to compensate for this faster pace, only the same rewards as the original Japanese server. RUN AWAY WHILE YOU STILL CAN!!

While I enjoy many aspects of Umamusume: Pretty Derby Global server, there are many drawbacks that make the experience tough for both free-to-play players and spenders. For context, I’m somewhere in-between: I spend within my limits and try to plan strategically, but I’m not naturally good at gacha games and often have to work around common hurdles. To clarify, there are four regional servers that are all different. Which are Japanese, Taiwanese, South Korean, and Global server. For example, The Global server is the only one with a 0.5% rate-up chance at the time of Kitasan Black's event banner. While the Japanese, Taiwanese, and South Korean servers had a 0.75% rate-up chance for the same banner at the time they had that event. In order for improvements to consistently be delivered properly. The community must always be proactive in positive & healthy ways to push the developers to provide us appropriate support. There are a few factors you must keep in mind when playing on the Global servers. This has not changed nor improved since release. Regardless of if this has already been addressed and 'fixed'. Does not always guarantee if they have genuinely resolved the technical issues effectively. [u] [h2] 1. The pity system feels outdated. [/h2] [/u] To guarantee a featured SSR or support card you need 200 pulls via Exchange Points, and pulls do not carry over between banners. Since most banners only last about a week, this target is unrealistic for many players. Missing out on a character or card you really want feels punishing compared to modern gacha standards, where soft pity or increasing odds are common. [u] [h2] 2. Event pacing is too aggressive. [/h2] [/u] Global’s event schedule is extremely fast, with fewer breaks (“dead weeks”) as the devs push to catch up to other servers. This leaves little time to gather resources like Carats. Players are forced to skip banners and events, even if they want to engage more, because the resource economy doesn’t support participation. [u] [h2] 3. Missing quality-of-life features. [/h2] [/u] Global lacks several tools, buffs, and improvements that are already present in Japanese, Taiwanese, and Korean servers (for example, certain race tools, accessibility options, and camera modes). This makes Global feel like a deliberately handicapped version of the game, even though there’s no clear reason why players here should have a worse experience. It has made the overall ecosystem frustrating & difficult that it takes away the positive experiences [u] [h2] 4. Harsh RNG and limited counterplay. [/h2] [/u] Negative status effects occur too frequently, and the infirmary tool doesn’t reliably remove them. As a result, even carefully planned runs can be ruined by bad luck. Combined with low gacha rates, this creates an environment that feels unfair and frustrating rather than challenging. [u] [h2] 5. Information gaps and miscommunication. [/h2] [/u] Another challenge is the lack of clear, accurate guidance for Global. Most community guides come from non-Global servers that already had quality-of-life updates, so their advice doesn’t always apply. Combined with limited in-game explanations, this leads to confusion, misinformation, and unnecessary frustration for new players. Developers could really help by providing better tutorials or Global-specific guidance so players don’t feel left behind. [u] [h2] Potential Solutions [/h2] [/u] [b] QoL Features First: [/b] Immediately patch in the tools, menus, buffs, and accessibility options already in JP (low risk, high reward). [b] Resource Economy Adjustments: [/b] Increase Carat rewards, add more free pulls, or reduce banner cost. [b] Pity System Modernization: [/b] Introduce soft pity or rollover points (like other gacha games). [b] Event Calendar Balance: [/b] Slightly slow the accelerated schedule, giving breathing room for resource gathering. Allow players to select multiple characters and/or support cards in order of most preferred to least where the list can be changed at any time. So if the player isn't having much luck to receive the rate-up. They can at least get the preferred characters and/or support cards they need. You can also offer packages to allow players to select any character and support card. [b] Official Global Guides: [/b] Release dev-made guides/videos tailored for Global mechanics (so misinformation drops). In short, while Umamusume: Pretty Derby Global has a fun core and strong potential, the current version still feels restricted, grind-heavy, and poorly supported compared to other servers. Without better communication, resource balancing, and feature parity, it risks alienating both new and veteran players alike.

Gemini Platinum Winner, and have been finalist in most CM (the End-Game PVP of this game). I have read the Comprehensive Google Doc, checked every wiki and played as optimally as possible. I’m burned out out of my mind with this game. TL;DR it’s a glorified gambling machine. The game is a roguelite where the main gameplay loop is taking care of your Uma by pressing buttons Tamagotchi style and gaining numbers and skills with their pros and cons attached to them. The bigger the numbers and the more the skills, the better. However, your Uma might get tired, and the more tired she is, the higher’s the chance you might fail, which can be a setback depending on the gravity of the failure. While you’re in a career, you can read a visual novel of your Uma’s story based on real events and the Scenario’s story, which is an additional overarching narrative that, in most cases, creates more mechanics for your Uma to improve. After finishing a career, these Umas are used in PVP settings to increase rank, win trophies and generally get more gacha points to pull for more horses. The Umas can also be used in future careers to create better horses using an inheritance system of skills and stats and, if your Uma has really good inheritance stats, you can share it with friends for them to use it (and you as well) a limited number of times a day. The worst elements of this game, and the sole reasons I’m uninstalling this game, are the PVP settings and the RNG of the entire game. With PVP, comes a meta, and as most games with a meta, it means there are a specific set of cards and horses that will be better than others. However, the more I play this game, the more I see the major issue I see with this game is that the real meta is seeing how big your wallet is or how lucky your account was in the first 200 - 300 pulls of your account. If you didn’t pull for these specific cards, you might as well forget playing, because you’re never catching up with the server. Literally thousands of gacha points unnaccessible because you didn’t use your wallet enough. And even if you do get the best cards in the game with the highest number of copies or whatever, you’re still subject to RNG everywhere. There are times in which, if you didnt get the correct event, the correct inspiration, the correct hint, the correct trainings, training boosts, heck if your horse just stood funny that turn and decided to get a Migraine or become a Slacker, the run can be considered over for competitive settings, and it’s literally out of your control and a waste of your time and daily resources. There are so many elements you have to balance at the same time that it becomes frustrating that, if one of these elements fails, the entire card castle that is a run in this game just falls. And EVEN THEN, if you have the perfect Uma with perfect score and perfect skills, the game has something called Wit and Condition checks that add even more RNG to a race. If your Uma fails a roll, or if the other horses decide to surround her, it most likely means that you’re losing that race. I literally won one of the most difficult PVP cups because of that, it was exhilarating; but I don’t think it was because my Uma was good. When the entire game relies on how lucky you are is when you realise the game is a glorified gambling addiction that gives you short bursts of dopamine between hours and hours and hours of frustration, misery and anxiety. I could be doing literally anything else with my life, play other games. The only redeeming factors are the character designs and personalities and the songs; but I can enjoy those watching the anime or seeing memes on social media. The stories are cliché and work sometimes; but it’s not a good enough reason to keep pulling the lever for the 777.

Summary: Umamusume is a decent Excel spreadsheet game that is completely unfriendly to casual players. With 240 hours in the game, I've reached the point where I finally comprehend just how much grinding this game requires in order to maximize the gameplay. The grind is due to the banner mechanics, which in my opinion are completely unfair to free-to-play players. Support cards and trainee banners are separate, which is fair enough, but the issue is that the game gives you barely any in-game currency. This leads to playing EVERY DAY for a MONTH to guarantee the card you want on ONE banner. Unlike other gacha games, Uma lacks any carry over points between banners, which means you can't spend on banners you want and use saved points on future banners. Instead, you HAVE to spend 200 pulls on one banner and you HAVE to skip out on other banners in order to save. And, because support cards are ultimately more important than trainees, you'll miss out on the single most fun part of the game (the trainees) all in the pursuit of getting cards that will improve your runs by mere margins. Sure, you could buy currency, but the exchange rate is worse than Clash Royale, and that's saying something ($20 gets you a single banner 10-pull in Uma, it's pathetic. For that price you could buy Hollow Knight, Enter the Gungeon, Dead Cells, the Binding of Isaac, or so many other objectively better games). The curtain fell apart for me when I finally faced the reality that I would have to spend up to an hour every day, of every month, to get what is essentially a math equation (the support card) that would increase my run outcomes by a measly couple of points, and would have to do this repeatedly for a year if I want to make a single viable deck for PVP or the whale-ridden hellscape that is Champion's Meet. And it's with that realization that I'm putting this game down, because life would be better spent playing ANY other game that gives meaningful rewards for the effort put in. Or maybe I'll pick up an actual hobby instead of racing horse girls. If you are at all interested in the gameplay, this game is not for you. The skill ceiling is low and largely reliant on RNG, and it quickly devolves into repeating almost the exact same run every single day, turning your precious gaming time into monotonous slop. If you're just here for the horse girls and don't care about the meta or even winning every run, then go crazy. The anime is pretty good tho, so some points for that I guess.

Every character in this game gets their own career run, and in the run you can get to understand them more, making part of the gameplay lore-motivated. Although yes some horses do get more story as per introduced in the anime, the minor characters still get the same amount of flesh. [h1]Do i need to pay[/h1]: F2P can still enjoy the game since the game is LARGELY single player mode, but i gotta say the mechanics are designed in the way to strongly encourage you to get more copies of a support card (you can think of it as weapons). Umamusume is a prime example of corporate greed, common among Japanese gacha games: a genuine love letter to Japanese horse racing with great production value ruined by predatory game design & monetization, and it continues to get worse because no one's pressuring Cygames to change. In fact, it already got worse on the JP server. [h3]1. RNG-heavy game design[/h3] The "Gambling" tag isn't just for show. The entire game, including racing, relies heavily on RNG. You can have the best support cards, the best parent umamusume & still lose to RNG. Career mode's RNG leans more toward the punishing side. [list] [*]Your trainee may randomly lose mood, forcing you to waste turns to raise them back if you don’t use Pal cards. [*]Resting has a chance to grant less energy, and a “Night Owl” debuff that causes your trainee to randomly lose mood. [*]Support cards often may not appear on crucial turns like summer training. [*]Many of the support card events that grant important skills have a chance not to appear at all, or not granting the desired skills, effectively "gluing" your runs. [/list] Legacy farming is like farming for decent gear in an RPG/looter shooter. There are so many layers of RNG that most of the parents you get are trash: [list] [*]Blue spark: 20% chance for 1 of the 5 stats, 5% to get 3* at 600 stats, 10% at 1200. [*]Red spark: randomly chosen between your character’s A-rank aptitudes [*]White spark: 20% for white skills, 25% for ◎ white, 40% for gold, increases by 2.5% when grandparents have it. [/list] This is a raising sim where you use the result of your career to PvP. In order to be competitive in PvP, on top of having good support cards, you need to repeatedly grind for good rolls if you want to win, and sometimes still gets beaten by those who high rolled. A scenario may be fun at first, but when the novelty wears off, the experience boils down to continously rolling in hope of “RNG will be better this time.” Most of the time, you didn’t do anything wrong. The game just randomly goes, “Hey, it’s time to screw this Torena up,” and decides to slap a middle finger in your face. [h3]2. The support card gacha[/h3] You cannot play this game without pulling support cards, as all support cards are useless at 0LB (Limit break), so useless that you can’t even consistently clear career with them. Most cards require 3LB/MLB in order to get the most value out of them. However, the support gacha: [list] [*]Only has 3% SSR rate, with 0.5% ~ 0.75% for rate-up cards, and is heavily diluted with useless cards. [*]Has no pity system. You can reach spark (200 pulls) without getting a single copy of the desired card, let alone MLB. [*]Spark progression resets when banner ends. [*]You can’t exchange cleats, the currency obtained by breaking duplicate MLBs, for LB crystals. Yet you can do so for the character gacha, where many characters are usable at 3*. [*]LB crystal shards are drip-fed at such a snail’s pace that you only get 1 crystal every 3-4 months. [*]Future scenarios come with specialized support cards, which are crucial for a smooth run, but are no longer viable when a new scenario arrives. [/list] That means the majority of your pulls will be spent on support cards until MLB. For a game where the main appeal lies in the characters, this is a huge bummer, as you can’t enjoy the characters’ stories without pulling them first. [h3]3. The illusion of generosity[/h3] Cygames employs a tactic also seen in their other titles like Granblue Fantasy or Dragalia Lost, where they frequently throw freebies at players as a marketing tool & to make themselves look generous. In exchange, they designed the game in a way to quickly burn through those freebies, while reducing the carat income from regular play. The gacha is diluted with mostly filler content: [list] [*]Character alts provide only 3 new story events related to their costumes & a new skill set [*]The majority of the support cards are useless, while still requiring multiple LBs to be viable. [/list] The daily missions give you 50 carats (0.33 pulls) per day, which is buffed to 75 (0.5 pulls) to accommodate the accelerated schedule. Modern KR/CN gacha games de-emphasize the importance of PvP. Those games usually only provide a small reward bump for higher rankings, or just don't have PvP at all. Umamusume, however, lures you into grinding PvP by designing it in a way that lets you earn more for higher achievements: [list] [*] Team Trials class 6 gives you 375 carats weekly, a major bump from 225 in class 5 [*] Champions' Meeting, a 3v3v3 event, gives you exponentially higher carats amount the more you win in an entry. 3/5 wins to qualify for Group A, with rewards going up to 2000 carats for winning Graded League Group A finals. [/list] The riches get richer. [h3]4. The "macrotransactions"[/h3] The $7 monthly carat subscription gives you 1500 free + 500 paid carats, equivalent to 13.33 pulls, which is lower compared to competitors like Genshin (16 pulls + 300 paid currency). Its value is significantly lower when combined with the bloated gacha & the accelerated schedule. During anniversaries, the game may sell selector tickets. These are highly sought after, as their value may be worth up to 200 pulls, and the chance to get “spooked” (getting desired non-rate-up units) in gacha is very low. The first ones cost $21, like most other gacha games. The second ones, however, are sold for a whopping $70, equal to a modern AAA game or 1.75 Arc Raiders. Since the 3rd Anniversary, the JP server has introduced step-up gacha that costs up to 5000 PAID carats per banner. Yes, you have to spend real-life money on them. On top of that, the JP server also paywalls QoL features: [list] [*]Spark reroll subscription, which makes rerolling sparks free instead of costing energy or 100 carats, the game’s premium currency. [*]Blue/Pink spark subscription, which allows the selection of blue/pink sparks for free instead of for 100 carats. [*]The recently introduced “Uma Plan” subscription that allows you to mass produce 5 parents (10 with spark reroll subscription), select one of 2 inspiration rolls during a career run, and +100 follow slots on first purchase. [/list] The devs knew that RNG & parent farming is a pain, but instead of fixing for everyone, they sell the medicine to alleviate the problem, widening the gap between F2P/Low spender & the dolphins/whales. The +100 borrow slots from Uma Plan are also a tactic Cygames uses to lure you into subscribing. They want you to get used to the QoLs you get from the subscription so that it feels bad to unsubscribe, because those QoLs are really, really good, which should have been free for everyone in the first place. [h3]The Ugly[/h3] Players know that the game is money-hungry, yet they don’t pressure the devs to improve it. Yes, I understand that you can enjoy the game in different ways. However. every time criticism about the game comes up, the "Tracen Vigilante Crew" tries to dismiss it with comments like "take a break" or "it's your fault" etc. Cygames isn't your friend, why do you keep defending them? Because there’s no other horse raising sim as good as Umamusume, the game basically has 0 competition. They can milk the fanbase however they want, and the JP crowd will still be willing to swipe their credit cards. Their parasocial relationship with the horse girls are so strong that they’re willing to be exploited by the devs just to see the girls happy. All it takes for people to chant “Glory to Cygames” is free pulls that look generous on the surface, but actually it’s like a drop in the ocean when combined with the stingy gacha. Who’s gonna tell them that the money CyberAgent uses to do philanthropy & sponsorships comes from predatory gaming practices? A good game should make me “want” to spend money to support the devs, not “need” to spend money in order to have a decent experience.

Uma Musume is one of the most powerful IPs to come out of Japan and one of the most significant gacha games as well. The biggest draw back is exactly that one thing that perpetually and continuously harms gacha games, the fact they are gacha games. I really enjoy Uma Musume as an IP overall, however. I never once really had any interest in equine sports, but now I feel like consuming all seasons, OVAs and movies of the anime, has truly given me an augmented appreciation for it all and what goes into it. My initial appreciation for Uma Musume actually goes back half a decade ago. When the Cinderella Gray manga was still being serialized. I actually bought a Chromebook for the exclusive purpose of using it as a glorified manga-tablet for reading just that manga at night. It was not a manga I was expecting to outright adore, given it was recommended to me by someone random anon on an image board. Yet, here I am years later, having watched the anime adaption and having played the game a bit. The makings of an absolutely perfect game is in the making here. I really hope one day we get a more polished, singleplayer driven variant that is equal parts virtual novel and sports management sim. All the actual gameplay mechanics are absolutely superb, addicting and even when RNG gets in the way, the actual gameplay loop is something that captures people very deeply. Combine that with the amazing characterizations for even single star horses like King Halo, every girl really feels like they have main character writing and energy. While hardly the most dynamic of career and storymodes, and with a very limited presentation scope, the fact that the commentary is fully voiced and so varied for every possible instance in a race is absolutely amazing. The production value behind the game in terms of this sort of immersive stuff greatly exceeds a lot of its peers. All in all, for a mobile game of its age, it still holds up and in many way, has more charm and spirit than a lot of the main competitors which have become Genshin slop and variants of it. As someone who has "beaten" Fate Grand Order and also Arknights and Dolls Frontline 1, I have to say that I simply do not have the time, patience or energy nor desire to engage in a grinding-gacha game ever again. Thus, my journey with the game ends with my failed initial career run with King Halo. But in those three hours, I appreciated a character and a horse I never knew of before. Sadly, the way the game is built, will always perpetually encourage constant replaying of the same content without variance due to a lot of the win states, even with generous chances on your side, is simply are mathematically out of your control. And it just so happens that every horse girl I want to play, has forum threads upon forum threads regarding how difficult it is to train them and just how much hyper meta knowledge is necessary to even bring them into a competitive fold. I really wish the game had a more open free career mode without story events or goals and really let us play more on the immersive sim side of things, but then, genuinely, that would be the only thing people would probably play. Still, the game is far from bad, but the IP is definitely more of something I prefer reading and watching than engaging in, as far as how this system works. But honestly, I can tell that for a lot of people, this game is basically the same kind of crack the CIA was handing out to disenfranchised neighborhoods in the late Cold War. Gold Ship is still the strongest character and horse in all of history.

TL;DR: Umamusume has a genuinely strong and satisfying training game buried under a progression system that is hostile to new and late players. You do not steadily grind toward the fun; you survive months of weak decks, scarce Carats, non-carrying 200-pull pity and duplicate-gated supports just to assemble the tools needed to play Career mode properly—while the meta continues moving ahead of you. Once your account is built, the game can be excellent. Building it from scratch is stagnant, exploitative and designed to make spending hundreds of dollars the only reliable way to bypass the waiting. Umamusume: A Strong Game Choked by Its Gacha Economy Umamusume has a genuinely good core: train characters through changing scenarios, build around support decks and inheritance, manage limited turns, and create different racers for different distances and strategies. The problem is that new players are not given fair access to that game. A fresh account can enter Career mode, but usually has one usable borrowed support and five weak, incomplete or mismatched cards. Most SSR supports are poor at low limit break, and many only become properly good around 3LB. Since MLB requires five total copies, pulling one SSR often gives you the name, artwork and events, but not a card strong enough to use. Support cards do not merely raise your final rank. They determine how the whole Career feels: bond speed, friendship training, training gains, support placement, Skill Point income, energy, mood, secondary stats and consistency. A weak deck makes the main game slower, flatter and less responsive even when the player knows what to do. Cygames does not merely sell extra power. It sells access to the more satisfying version of Career mode. The starting progression is also badly designed. Playing more Careers does not reliably solve the support deficit. Career mode gives trained Umas, fans, inheritance and finite mission rewards, but it does not provide a dependable repeatable path to current supports or limit breaks. The resources that matter—Carats, selectors and limit-break materials—are restricted by events, campaigns, logins and time. So the early game is less “grinding” and more surviving: Play with a poor deck, exhaust the available Carats, skip most banners, wait until you have enough for 200 pulls, wait for a banner strong enough to justify spending everything, then hope you pull enough copies for the card to become usable. The 200-pull pity is not generous protection. It is a hard commitment threshold. At 200 pulls you may select one featured copy. At 199, you cannot, and the progress does not meaningfully carry into a future banner. Worse, one pity guarantees only one copy. It does not guarantee 3LB, MLB, or even a card strong enough to enter the deck. Even 400 pulls guarantee only two exchange copies. A support needing four or five total copies can still remain incomplete after an enormous investment. One successful banner is nowhere near enough. A deck uses six supports. Even with one borrowed card, a new player still needs several owned supports that work together. Completing one card may leave the deck as one strong borrow, one strong owned card and four weak slots. Then the player must save again, wait again and gamble again across several more banners. The real entry requirement is not “save for one good banner.” It is “survive until several deeply funded banners have assembled most of a functional deck.” The economy also punishes experimentation. Because Carats are scarce and low-LB SSRs are weak, the rational strategy is to ignore most banners, avoid favourite characters if support growth matters, follow tier lists, hoard for months and dump everything into a small number of meta supports. For a game whose depth comes from deck building, its economy discourages players from exploring that deck building. The catch-up race is unfair because the target keeps moving. While a new player saves, scenarios change, preferred deck structures change, stronger supports arrive and old targets lose value. Veterans already own completed cards and can keep playing while evaluating replacements. New players are saving toward relevance while the definition of relevance moves forward. Old completed cards depreciate, new first copies are weak, replacing them requires deep duplicate investment, and those replacements will eventually depreciate too. The system does not preserve player investment. It creates repeated reasons to reinvest. Rental supports and fixed rental decks are workarounds, not solutions. They prove that a stronger starting experience is possible, but borrowed access does not build the player’s collection or give them real freedom. Once an account owns a coherent support core, Umamusume becomes much better. Career decisions matter, strong training turns happen, scenarios can be explored properly, builds become flexible and optimisation becomes enjoyable. But reaching that state from scratch—especially years after launch—is slow, stagnant, luck-dependent and exploitative. The game’s best form is placed behind months of waiting, extreme saving discipline, favourable duplicate luck or substantial spending. Cygames could fix the problem by making 0LB cards functional, moving key effects earlier, carrying pity between banners, giving more universal limit-break materials, improving repeatable Carat income or providing permanent competitive starter supports. Instead, it adds rentals (a feature in the JP version not in global, which partially and temporarily solves the entry gate problem of new players), free pulls, selectors and special banners that reduce abandonment while preserving the pressure to spend. That is not an accident. It is the business model. The honest verdict: Umamusume is not merely slow for beginners. Its progression is structurally hostile to late entrants. Playing more does not reliably solve the support deficit. Pity is a non-carrying 200-pull cliff. One pity guarantees only one often-incomplete copy. Most strong supports need several copies. One banner cannot build a deck. The meta advances while the player saves, and spending is the only reliable way to compress the process. Umamusume becomes a good game after the account is built. Building that account from scratch is the part designed to wear players down and monetise their impatience. Cygames does not merely sell advantages above the gameplay floor. It keeps the floor low, then sells players the means to climb high enough for the game to feel properly playable.
